questions.topic: Recognising the shape that calls for trig substitution
questions.learningObjective: identify which radical shapes call for a trigonometric substitution
questions.stem: Which of these four indefinite integrals is the one that calls for a trigonometric substitution?

options.text: The integral of the square root of 9 minus x squared with respect to x
The integral of 1 over the quantity 1 plus x squared with respect to x
options.misconception: applies a trig substitution where the arctangent antiderivative is already the answer

options.text: The integral of x cubed minus 3x plus 2 with respect to x
options.misconception: looks for a radical to remove in a polynomial that has none

options.text: The integral of the exponential of negative x squared with respect to x
options.misconception: treats an exponential as if it hid a quadratic radical underneath

questions.explanation: A trigonometric substitution is worth setting up only when a square root of a quadratic sits in the denominator or under the radical and no algebraic trick removes it. The square root of 9 minus x squared is exactly that shape. The other three cases are already solved by simpler tools: 1 over 1 plus x squared is the arctangent, a plain polynomial needs only the power rule, and an exponential of a square needs the chain rule alone. Substituting a sine into any of those would make the work longer, not shorter.
questions.hint: Ask which integrand hides a square root that no algebraic substitution can clear.

options.misconception: swaps the secant and tangent substitutions, which fit the plus and minus radicals respectively

questions.explanation: Each pairing is forced by the Pythagorean identity that the engine of the whole method. The identity the sine squared plus the cosine squared equals 1 turns a squared constant minus x squared into a squared cosine when x equals a times the sine of theta. The identity one plus the tangent squared equals the secant squared does the same job for x squared plus a squared constant, and the identity the secant squared minus the tangent squared equals 1 handles x squared minus a squared constant. Choosing the other way round reintroduces the very radical being removed.
questions.hint: Each radical is a rearrangement of one of the three Pythagorean identities.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Recognising the shape that calls for trig substitution
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which a trigonometric substitution removes a radical
questions.stem: Explain in a few sentences why substituting x equals 3 times the sine of theta converts the radical in the square root of 9 minus x squared into a cosine.

answer.exemplar: The substitution makes x squared equal to 9 times the sine squared of theta, so 9 minus x squared becomes 9 of one minus the sine squared of theta, which is 9 times the cosine squared of theta by the identity that the sine squared plus the cosine squared equals 1. The square root of that is 3 times the cosine of theta, on the branch where the cosine is positive, so the radical has become a bare trig function. What is left is an integral in theta involving only sines and cosines, which the power rule and the half-angle identity can finish. The constant 3 has to travel along through the differential, and the cosine of theta must finally be rewritten in terms of x to return the answer to the original variable.

questions.explanation: Substitution is a rewriting device, not a trick: it exchanges an algebraic difficulty for a trigonometric one that is already solved. Once x equals 3 times the sine of theta, the quantity 9 minus x squared is literally 9 times the cosine squared of theta, so its square root is 3 times the cosine of theta, up to a sign fixed by choosing the branch. The integral is now an ordinary trigonometric integral, and the half-angle identity reduces even the stubborn squared trigonometric functions to first powers. Two obligations remain before the answer is finished: the differential picks up the factor 3, and the angle has to be eliminated in favour of x again.
questions.hint: Expand the substitution inside the radical and apply the sine-cosine squares identity.

The first term is x times the square root of 9 minus x squared, plus 9 times the arcsine of x over 3

options.misconception: invents a coefficient unrelated to the constant 3 in the radicand

questions.explanation: Substituting x equals 3 times the sine of theta turns the radical into 3 times the cosine of theta and the differential into 3 times the cosine of theta times d-theta, so the integrand becomes 9 of the cosine squared of theta, which the half-angle identity splits into a constant part and a double-angle part. The leftover 3 of theta is 3 times the arcsine of x over 3, and the coefficient 9 over 2 comes from the 9 in the radicand divided by 2.
questions.hint: The coefficient of the arcsine term is the constant in the radicand divided by 2.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate a definite integral of a quarter-circle integrand by sine substitution
questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral of the square root of 9 minus x squared between 0 and 2, and report the result to six decimal places.
questions.explanation: Substitute x equals 3 times the sine of theta, so the upper limit becomes the arcsine of 2 over 3, which is 0.729728, and the integrand with its differential becomes 9 of the cosine squared of theta. Using the half-angle identity, the antiderivative is 9 of theta over 2 plus 9 of the sine of twice theta over 4. At the upper limit the sine of twice theta is 2 of the sine times the cosine, that is 2 times 2 over 3 times the square root of 5 over 3, so the algebraic part contributes 9 of 2 over 3 times 2 over 3 times the square root of 5 over 3, which is the square root of 5, giving 4.5 times 0.729728 plus 4.5 times 0.496904, a total of 5.519842. The full quarter circle of radius 3 would be 9 pi over 4, that is 7.068583, so the value is sensibly smaller.
questions.hint: Convert the upper limit to the arcsine of 2 over 3 before integrating.

questions.explanation: Substitute x equals the sine of theta, so the differential becomes the cosine of theta d-theta, and the square root of 1 minus x squared becomes the cosine of theta on this interval. The whole integrand therefore collapses to the sine squared of theta d-theta, and the limits run from 0 to pi over 2. The half-angle identity splits the sine squared into 1 minus the cosine of twice theta over 2, whose antiderivative is theta over 2 minus the sine of twice theta over 4. At pi over 2 the sine of pi is 0, leaving pi over 4, that is 0.785398, the same as a quarter of the area under the unit circle.
questions.hint: After the substitution the integrand is the sine squared, not the cosine squared.

questions.topic: Trigonometric identities used in substitution
questions.learningObjective: apply the half-angle identity to finish a trigonometric integral
questions.stem: Give an antiderivative with respect to theta of the cosine of theta squared, expressed without any squared trigonometric function.

answer.exemplar: The antiderivative is theta over 2 plus the sine of twice theta over 4, plus a constant of integration. It comes from the half-angle identity that the cosine squared of theta equals 1 plus the cosine of twice theta, all divided by 2, which turns a squared trigonometric function into a constant plus a first-power one. The constant half integrates to theta over 2, and the half of the cosine of twice theta integrates, by the chain rule, to the sine of twice theta over 4. This is precisely the step that lets a trigonometric substitution finish: without the half-angle identity a squared cosine is stuck, because the power rule does not apply to a trigonometric function.

questions.explanation: A trigonometric substitution is only worth doing if the trigonometric integral that results can actually be finished, and the step that guarantees this is the half-angle identity. It rewrites a squared trigonometric function as a constant plus a first-power one, so the power rule becomes applicable to half of the integrand while the other half is handled by the chain rule. Working the identity through, half of the constant integrates to half of the angle and half of the cosine of twice the angle integrates to a quarter of the sine of twice the angle.
questions.hint: Replace the squared cosine by a constant plus a cosine of twice the angle.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Trigonometric identities used in substitution
questions.learningObjective: explain why a trigonometric substitution needs a half-angle identity at the end
questions.stem: Explain why a substitution such as x equals 3 times the sine of theta leaves work that only the half-angle identity can finish.

answer.exemplar: After the substitution the radical has been traded for a bare trigonometric function, but the integrand now contains a squared one, for example 9 of the cosine squared of theta. The power rule, which is what settles any algebraic integrand, does not apply to a trigonometric function, because the chain rule would then demand integrating the cosine, and that is circular. The half-angle identity breaks the deadlock by rewriting the squared cosine as a constant plus a cosine of twice the angle, both of which the power rule and the chain rule handle. Without it the substitution has merely moved the difficulty from algebra to trigonometry rather than removing it.

questions.explanation: The point of a substitution is to remove difficulty, not to relocate it, and the half-angle identity is the step that completes the removal. What is left after the substitution is a squared trigonometric function, and the power rule is powerless there because treating the cosine as a variable would immediately require integrating a cosine, which is precisely what is already being done. The identity that the squared cosine is a constant plus a cosine of twice the angle breaks that circularity, producing one term the power rule can take and one term the chain rule can take.
questions.hint: Ask why the power rule cannot be applied directly to a squared trigonometric function.

questions.topic: A definite integral whose bounds reach an improper endpoint
questions.learningObjective: decide when a definite integral must be treated as improper
questions.stem: When must a definite integral be evaluated as a limit rather than by the fundamental theorem?

options.text: When the integrand becomes unbounded at or inside an endpoint of the interval of integration
When the antiderivative cannot be written in closed form, which happens for almost every integrand
options.misconception: believes a missing closed form forces a limit treatment, when numerical methods handle that case

options.text: When the interval of integration extends past the point where the integrand first equals zero
options.misconception: confuses a zero of the integrand with an unbounded integrand, which behave quite differently

options.text: When the value of the integrand at an endpoint is irrational, which has no bearing on convergence
options.misconception: believes the arithmetic type of an endpoint value affects whether an integral converges

questions.explanation: The fundamental theorem needs the integrand to be continuous on the closed interval of integration, and the only way that can fail is through unbounded behaviour at an endpoint or inside the interval, so that is exactly the condition for treating the integral as improper. A zero of the integrand is harmless, since a continuous function vanishing at a point is perfectly integrable there, and a missing closed form is a separate inconvenience handled by approximation. Convergence of the resulting limit is a separate question that must be checked in its own right.
questions.hint: Ask whether the integrand is continuous on the whole closed interval.

questions.stem: A solution reaches 9 of the squared cosine of theta, rewrites the squared cosine as 1 plus the cosine of twice the angle over 2, and obtains a final answer with the wrong sign. Where does it start to fail?

The identity is written correctly, so the error lies in the chain rule applied to the cosine of twice the angle
options.misconception: clears the identity and blames the integration step that follows it

options.text: The identity is written correctly, so the error lies in the choice of the plus logarithmic form rather than the minus form
options.misconception: reaches for a log-form explanation when the fault is in the trig identity

options.text: The identity is written correctly, so the error must be a rounding slip in the final decimal
options.misconception: assumes a sign error is really a numerical one

questions.explanation: The half-angle identity may be written either as the squared cosine being 1 plus the cosine of twice the angle over 2 or, equivalently, as 1 minus the sine squared over 2. questions.stem: Which expression is the linearization of a function f at a base point a?

Substituting f of x into the formula instead would smuggle the unknown back in, and leaving the slope as a function of x would give a curve rather than a line.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_I
questions.topic: Differentials and relative error
questions.learningObjective: write the differential of a polynomial
questions.stem: Write the differential of the function given by x squared plus 3x, and give its value at the point where x equals 2.

answer.exemplar: The differential is the quantity 2x plus 3 times dx, and at the point where x equals 2 its value is 7 of dx. The differential of a single-variable function is by definition its derivative multiplied by a small change in the independent variable, so nothing else is involved: the chain rule does not apply because there is only one variable. The reason this matters is that the differential is the first-order model of the actual change, so an increment of dx at a point produces a change of about 2x plus 3 of dx, with an error that grows like the square of the increment.

questions.explanation: For a function of a single variable the differential is simply the derivative times a small change in the input, so the whole computation is a derivative. The power rule gives 2x plus 3, and multiplying by the change dx gives the differential, whose value at x = 2 is 7 of dx. The point of the differential is that it captures the change to first order, so it is the right tool for propagating a small measurement error, and the neglected error is of second order in the increment.
questions.hint: The differential of a function of one variable is its derivative times a small change in the input.
